questions.question: How does Java source code achieve the "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA) capability?
options: Because the `javac` compiler compiles `.java` files directly into universal Machine Code for all CPUs.
Because `javac` compiles source code into intermediate Bytecode (`.class` files), and the OS-specific JVM (Windows, Linux, macOS) interprets and JIT-compiles that bytecode into native machine code.
Because every computer uses the exact same Intel processor.
Because Java runs entirely inside a web browser just like JavaScript.
questions.explanation: Bytecode is hardware-independent virtual machine code. Each operating system has its own JVM implementation that translates standardized Bytecode into native machine instructions.
questions.card_front: How does Java source code achieve the "Write Once, Run Anywhere" (WORA) capability?
questions.card_back: Because `javac` compiles source code into intermediate Bytecode (`.class` files), and the OS-specific JVM (Windows, Linux, macOS) interprets and JIT-compiles that bytecode into native machine code.

Original source code text compressed in ZIP format.
Linux Assembly language instructions.
questions.explanation: A `.class` file contains binary Bytecode conforming to the Java Virtual Machine Specification. Any compliant JVM can load, verify, and execute it regardless of the OS where it was compiled.

questions.card_back: Standardized intermediate Java Bytecode that the JVM can load, verify, and execute.

questions.question: What is the technical nature of the `var` keyword (introduced in Java 10), and how does it differ from `var` in JavaScript?
questions.code_snippet:
var ticketPrice = 150_000;
// ticketPrice = "FREE"; // Is this line valid?
options: `var` turns Java into a Dynamically Typed language, allowing `ticketPrice` to be reassigned to `"FREE"` at any time like JavaScript.
`var` is purely syntactic sugar for Local Variable Type Inference: the static type (`int`) is inferred and locked at compile time; reassigning `ticketPrice = "FREE"` causes a Compile-time Error.
`var` is a new JVM runtime data type equivalent to `Object` that auto-unboxes at runtime.
`var` degrades runtime performance because the JVM must guess types dynamically.
questions.explanation: In Java, `var` (JEP 286) is Local Variable Type Inference, not dynamic typing. Java remains 100% statically typed: `javac` infers `int` at compile time and emits the exact same bytecode as `int ticketPrice = 150_000;`.

The application attempted to access an uninitialized Lazy relationship after the Hibernate Session / `@Transactional` Persistence Context managing that entity had already closed (e.g., inside a Controller or view layer).
The field was annotated with `@Transient`.
Database username and password were not configured.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@Mock` and `@Spy` in Mockito?
options: `@Mock` creates a complete dummy shell where unstubbed methods return default values (`null`, `0`, `false`); `@Spy` wraps a real object instance, invoking real methods unless a specific method is explicitly stubbed.
`@Mock` only works on interfaces, whereas `@Spy` only works on abstract classes.
`@Spy` runs 5 times faster than `@Mock`.
`@Mock` stores data in a database, whereas `@Spy` stores data in RAM.
questions.explanation: A `@Mock` replaces all behavior with empty stubs by default. A `@Spy` (partial mock) delegates calls to the underlying real object unless overridden with `doReturn(...).when(spy).method()`.

questions.question: In JWT security architecture, why is an Access Token designed with a short lifespan (e.g., 15 minutes) while a Refresh Token has a longer lifespan (e.g., 7 days)?
options: Because a longer Access Token TTL makes the Base64 string too large to send over HTTP.

Because JWT Access Tokens are stateless (not looked up in a server session store on every request), a short TTL limits the window of damage if stolen; the Refresh Token is stored securely (and can be revoked/blacklisted in Redis) to issue new Access Tokens.
Because the HMAC-SHA256 algorithm mathematically expires after 15 minutes.
Because web browsers automatically delete all tokens every 15 minutes.
questions.explanation: Stateless JWT Access Tokens remain valid until expiration once signed. Keeping their TTL short (15m) minimizes exposure if leaked, while the Refresh Token can be validated against Redis or database revocation lists.

questions.question: How does Optimistic Locking (`@Version`) work in Spring Data JPA?
options: The database physically locks the row from the moment it is read until the transaction ends.

No physical DB lock is held during read; on update, Hibernate includes the `@Version` column in the `WHERE` clause (`UPDATE seats SET status=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?`). If another transaction incremented `version` first, 0 rows are updated and Hibernate throws `OptimisticLockingFailureException`.
Automatically broadcasts a WebSocket message whenever a user views a seat.
Allows reads but blocks all writes across the entire table for 10 minutes.
questions.explanation: Optimistic Locking avoids holding physical database locks during reads. At commit time, it checks whether the `@Version` number in the database still matches the version read initially; if not, it throws `OptimisticLockingFailureException`.

questions.question: What is the "Cache Stampede" (Dogpiling) phenomenon, and how is it mitigated in Ticket Station?
options: Redis runs out of memory and wipes all keys.

When a very "hot" cache key (e.g., today’s featured concert) expires (TTL reaches 0), thousands of concurrent requests miss the cache simultaneously and slam the Database to recompute it, crashing the DB; mitigate with TTL jitter, mutex locks on cache rebuild, or proactive background cache warming.
The network cable between Spring Boot and Redis is unplugged.
Cached data never expires.
questions.explanation: Cache Stampede happens when a hot key expires under heavy traffic and thousands of threads hit the database at once. Solutions include adding random jitter to TTLs, using a distributed mutex lock so only 1 thread rebuilds the cache, or refreshing the cache asynchronously before expiry.

options: It persists both the `orders` update and an `outbox_events` record inside the SAME local ACID database transaction; a background Relay Worker or Debezium CDC then reads `outbox_events` and reliably publishes to Kafka.

questions.question: Why should Production deployments use a Multi-Stage Dockerfile and run the container as a non-root user (`USER appuser`)?

# Stage 1: Build
FROM maven:3.9.6-eclipse-temurin-21-alpine AS builder
...
# Stage 2: Runtime
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser
COPY --from=builder /app/target/*.jar app.jar

options: Multi-stage builds separate the heavy build environment (Maven, JDK, source code, `.m2` cache) from the minimal JRE runtime image, shrinking image size from ~800MB+ down to ~150MB; running as a non-root user prevents container privilege escalation attacks on the host.

questions.explanation: Multi-Stage Dockerfiles leave build tools and source code behind, shipping only the compiled JAR inside a slim JRE image. Running as a non-root user adheres to CIS Docker Security Benchmarks by limiting damage if a vulnerability is exploited.
